title: The Portuguese Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Portugués from Porto
author: CaminoPlus
rights: © 2026 CaminoPlus. All rights reserved. Passages quoted from the classics are in the public domain and are credited where they appear.
ai_disclosure: Written with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), under the direction of CaminoPlus. Facts in the guides are listed with their sources; routes, closures and services change, so check local information before you walk.

spans.t: The Portuguese Way runs from the cathedral of Porto, on the Douro, to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. On the way it crosses a river that is also a border, the Minho, and passes from one language into two. This book follows the Central route, ~240 km in the CaminoPlus catalog, in eleven walking days.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this is your Camino, what each of the eleven days asks of you, and what to check before you leave home.
How to use it

If you are a month or more away, read the next four chapters in order: the Way in brief, whether it suits you, when to go, and what to do before you go. Then read the days, which are grouped by region, and the chapter on other ways to split them, which also gives the rule for the Compostela.
If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. Each day says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause, and where to take care.
If you are only dreaming, start with "Is this Camino for you?" and finish with "The inner Way". You can decide the rest later.
What this book is not

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts. They change from season to season, and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.

It is also not a walker's memoir. This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.
Every distance carries a tilde,
, because it is approximate. Where something depends on the season (a diversion, heat, a river after rain), the book says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Caminho
is the Portuguese word for "way" or "road", and
Camino
the Spanish; the route has both names. The greeting between pilgrims is
Buen Camino
in Spanish and
bom caminho
in Portuguese. A
peregrino
(Spanish and Portuguese alike) is a pilgrim. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card you carry and have stamped along the way; a stamp is a
sello
in Spanish and a
carimbo
in Portuguese. The
Compostela
is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules.
They are explained again when they first matter, and used plainly after that.
Pack lightly, walk gently, and take your time over the long hill.
Bom caminho.
Where it starts and ends

The Central route of the Portuguese Way starts at the Sé, the cathedral of Porto, and ends at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela. It heads north through Barcelos and Ponte de Lima to Valença, crosses the Minho by the International Bridge into Tui, and then runs through O Porriño, Redondela, Pontevedra, Caldas de Reis and Padrón. The cathedral of Santiago is the last building you reach.

The CaminoPlus catalog gives the length as ~240 km. Other sources differ, because they start from different points and count different paths. The Confraternity of St James says ~252 km from Porto, and Wikipedia says ~260 km. The Xunta de Galicia, the regional government, gives ~119 km for the Galician part from Tui. The eleven days in this book, measured as the stage chapters explain, add up to ~246 km. Treat every figure as a good guide and not as a measurement.
The eleven days follow the CaminoPlus stage list:

items.t: Day 1: Porto to Vilarinho, ~27 km
Day 2: Vilarinho to Barcelos, ~27 km
Day 3: Barcelos to Ponte de Lima, ~34 km
Day 4: Ponte de Lima to Rubiães, ~18 km
Day 5: Rubiães to Tui, ~21 km
Day 6: Tui to O Porriño, ~18 km
Day 7: O Porriño to Redondela, ~16 km
Day 8: Redondela to Pontevedra, ~18 km
Day 9: Pontevedra to Caldas de Reis, ~23 km
Day 10: Caldas de Reis to Padrón, ~19 km
Day 11: Padrón to Santiago de Compostela, ~25 km

spans.t: Stage plans vary a great deal on this road. The CaminoPlus route list speaks of twelve stages, because published plans divide the first days of the walk in different ways, and some end a day in Valença instead of Tui. This book follows the eleven-day list. A later chapter shows how to cut it differently.
What it feels like

It is a road of small rivers and stone bridges. In Portugal you cross the Cávado at Barcelos and the Lima at Ponte de Lima, and climb a ridge between them; then the Minho, the border, with a fortress on one bank and a cathedral on the other. In Galicia the road keeps within reach of the sea, with the head of the Ría de Vigo beside you on Day 8, before it turns inland to cross the Ulla at Padrón.

The Confraternity describes the route as following secondary and minor roads, with stretches of farm track and forest. It also warns that the Central route follows a main transport corridor, so it meets national roads, and the current route often joins them at the entrance and exit of towns. Expect road surfaces as well as woods, and a long first day through the suburbs of Porto.

The waymarking is generous. The Confraternity says yellow arrows are plentiful from Porto cathedral to the Portuguese border, thanks to the Associação dos Amigos do Caminho Português de Santiago, and that in Galicia granite pillars add the distance to Santiago to the arrows.
Why it exists

The Xunta says this road grew in importance from the twelfth century, after Portugal became independent. It follows older roads, among them the Roman Via XIX, which the Xunta dates to the first century AD and which linked Braga with Astorga through Ponte de Lima, Tui, Pontevedra, Santiago and Lugo.

Kings and queens took it. The Xunta names Elizabeth of Portugal, the "Holy Queen", who made a pilgrimage in the fourteenth century and offered her crown at the altar of St James; the Confraternity gives her years as 1271 to 1336 and calls her Queen Isabel. It also names Manuel I, who walked from Lisbon to Santiago in 1502. Portugal's north to south road network, the Xunta adds, was organised around the pilgrimage. And in the nineteenth century, when pilgrim numbers were at their lowest, the Portuguese Way was the busiest of the routes: more than eighty per cent of the foreign pilgrims that century were Portuguese.
Company on the road

Wikipedia, reporting the Pilgrim's Office statistics, says that in 2025 the Portuguese Way was the second most walked route to Santiago after the French Way, with 19 per cent of pilgrims. Of those who received the Compostela, 41 per cent started in Tui, 26 per cent in Porto and 18 per cent in Valença. Most finish between May and September.
Read together, those figures suggest that many people join at or near the border, so the road may feel quieter in Portugal than in Galicia. That is a reading of the statistics, not a promise.
How hard is it?

Not very, by the standards of the long Caminos, and not nothing. The Xunta rates the Galician part of the route "Medium-Low" overall, and rates its six stages from Tui as Low or Medium. There are no mountains. Two places are singled out for difficulty. In Portugal, Wikipedia calls the Labruja hills, on Day 4, one of the most tiring parts of the inland route. In Galicia, the Xunta marks the three sections of Day 6, out of Tui, Medium-High, its highest rating on the route, though it rates the whole stage Low.

What makes the Portuguese Way demanding is less the height than the length of some days and the surface. Day 3 is ~34 km, the longest in this book. Much of the walking is on minor roads and paved paths, and the route meets national roads, as the Confraternity of St James warns, especially where it enters and leaves towns. Your feet will notice before your lungs do.
Who it suits

It suits a first-time walker who has trained a little and wants a Camino with a clear shape: a start at a cathedral, a border in the middle, an arrival at another cathedral. The days run from ~16 to ~34 km, and eleven of them, with a rest day or two, fit inside a fortnight. The road passes through many towns between the stage towns, so a day can be cut short. The app and local advice will tell you where to sleep.

It suits people who like their history in stone. The road crosses medieval bridges, passes a Romanesque church at Rates, runs along sections of a Roman road, and goes through the old centres of Ponte de Lima, Tui and Pontevedra.

It suits people who want company. The Pilgrim's Office statistics, as Wikipedia reports them, put the Portuguese Way second among the routes to Santiago in 2025. Alone is possible, but you will have to choose your hours and your season.
Who might choose another

If you want solitude and silence, think about the season. Most pilgrims finish between May and September, according to the same statistics, and many join at or near the border, so the Galician half is likely to be the busier.
If you want mountains, forests without roads, or a high pass, this is not that Camino. The French Way, ~773 km in the catalog, crosses the Pyrenees, the Meseta and the mountains of León.
If you want the sea, take the Coastal variant, which leaves the Central route near Porto and rejoins it at Redondela. It has a book of its own in this series,
The Coastal Way
, and this book does not describe it.

If you have only a week, the Galician half is the short version: the Xunta's six stages from Tui to Santiago, ~119 km. Whether a start in Tui, Valença or anywhere else counts for the Compostela is a question for the Pilgrim's Office, and the chapter on other ways to split the days gives the Office's rule.
Questions worth asking yourself

items.t: Can you walk ~20 km on a hard surface, two or three days in a row, with your pack?
Is the long Day 3 acceptable, or will you split it? The next chapters show how.
Do you want the whole road from Porto, or the border and Galicia?
What do you want from the walk: sport, solitude, history, a rest, prayer, a promise kept? Every answer is a good one, and the road does not ask.

spans.t: If most of your answers are yes, and the others are "we shall see", you are ready for the next chapter.

This is a green road, and it is green because it rains. The Confraternity of St James describes northern Portugal and Galicia as a changeable maritime climate, where westerly winds bring generous rain, hence "Green Portugal" and "Green Spain". Everything below is a pattern, not a forecast.
The seasons
Spring.

The Confraternity calls spring a rewarding time, cool, with fresh growth. It is also still wet: at Porto airport the rainfall is ~100 mm in March and in April, and at Santiago ~140 mm and ~130 mm (averages for 1991 to 2020). Carry a proper rain jacket and a plan for wet feet.
Summer.

Wikipedia says most pilgrims finish this Camino between May and September, and the Confraternity warns that summer can be hot and humid, with the peak holiday months crowded. The averages are mild: in July and August the mean daytime high is ~24 to ~25 °C at both Porto airport and Santiago. The averages hide the extremes. The record highs are ~38.6 °C at Porto airport and ~39.4 °C at Santiago airport, and rain is scarce: ~17 mm in July at Porto, ~31 mm at Santiago. A heatwave on a long day, such as Day 3, is a safety matter, not a discomfort.
Autumn.

The Confraternity says early autumn is regarded as fairly dry and settled. By October the rain has returned: Porto averages ~149 mm and Santiago ~214 mm, the wettest month of the year at Santiago, and November is about as wet.
Winter.

Mild and damp. The mean daytime high in January is ~14 °C at Porto and ~12 °C at Santiago, with mean lows of ~6 °C and ~5 °C. Wikipedia says frost at Santiago is common only from December to February, about thirteen days a year, and that snow is uncommon, two or three days a year. The trouble in winter is not cold but rain and short days. The rainfall in January is ~150 mm at Porto and ~196 mm at Santiago.

The Confraternity adds that during periods of low pressure the rain can be heavy and prolonged, and that walkers should be adequately prepared. Wikipedia's infobox gives the walking season as March to October. Winter walks happen; they ask for a lighter plan and more patience.
Daylight

At the winter solstice there are about nine hours of daylight in Porto, and about the same in Santiago. At the summer solstice there are about fifteen. The clocks add a twist: Portugal keeps Western European Time and Galicia Central European Time, so the clock jumps forward one hour when you cross the border. Computed for each city, the winter sun rises at about eight o'clock in Porto and about nine o'clock in Santiago, and in June sets at about ten past nine in Porto and a quarter past ten in Santiago, by the local clock. In December, plan to finish before the light goes, at about five o'clock in Porto and about six in Santiago.
A month, in a line each

items.t: March and April:
cool and fresh, and wet.
May and June:
mild, with daytime highs of ~20 to ~23 °C at both ends, and the days at their longest.
July and August:
hot and dry, and crowded in the peak holiday months, as the Confraternity says; start early.
September:
warm, with the rain beginning to return: ~68 mm at Porto, ~89 mm at Santiago.
October and November:
wet, with the days shortening.
December to February:
the coldest and shortest days, with rain. If the statistics are a guide, few pilgrims finish then.

spans.t: Check before you go

Before any date, look for diversions, closures and, in summer, heat and fire warnings. The Confraternity says road works are still met on the route and are usually marked with a diversion. A path can change between this book's date and your walk.
The credencial
The
credencial

is your pilgrim's passport, and you need one before the first stamp. The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago says the official model is a cardboard card of sixteen concertina-folded pages, with boxes for the stamps. You can ask for it in person at the Office or at institutions the cathedral has authorised: parish churches, associations of friends of the Way, pilgrim hostels, confraternities. The Office lists where, by country, region and city, and it is worth looking before you leave home.

The Office gives the credencial two practical purposes: access to the hostels of the Way, and proof when you ask for the Compostela. It adds that the credencial "does not generate any rights". The stamps are normally collected where you sleep, and also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. The Office describes a digital credential too, as a phone app. Ask the Office what it accepts, and carry the paper card in any case.
Getting there

Porto has an international airport ~11 km northwest of the centre of the city, and Wikipedia says it has a station on line E of the Porto Metro. The Confraternity of St James adds that you can also fly into Lisbon, Vigo or Santiago and use public transport. Santiago airport is ~12 km east of the city.

The Confraternity notes a regular bus service between Santiago and Porto, of about four hours' journey, which makes it possible to fly into and out of the same city. Timetables change, so check the current ones when you plan your return.
Choosing your start
Where you begin sets the length of your walk. On this book's figures:

items.t: From Porto:
eleven days, ~246 km, the whole road, beginning at the cathedral, the Sé.
From Ponte de Lima:
eight days, ~158 km, which keeps the border, the Spanish towns and the arrival, and skips the long Day 3.
From Tui:
six days, ~119 km, the Xunta's six Galician stages.

spans.t: Add a rest day or two, and a day each to travel there and back, and the Porto start is about a fortnight. If you are choosing a start with the Compostela in mind, read the rule in the chapter on other ways to split the days first, and ask the Pilgrim's Office. No starting town in this book is a guarantee.
Training

Nobody needs to be an athlete for this road. The best preparation is also the dullest: walk, in the shoes and with the pack you will carry, on a hard surface, for two or three days in a row, and build up to the length of your longest planned day. Eleven days of ~16 to ~34 km ask a lot of a body that has not walked far in months. A few weeks of regular walking will do more than any programme.
Shoes and feet

Much of the road is minor roads and paved paths, with stretches of track and forest. Look for shoes with a cushioned sole and a little room in the toe box, because feet swell as the day goes on. Break them in before you leave. Two pairs of socks, changed at lunch, are a cheap defence against blisters. Treat a hot spot when you feel it, not when it has become a blister. If something hurts in a way that grows and does not fade, rest it, and see a doctor.
Packing

Pack light, and then lighter. The essentials are plain: a rain jacket, because this is a green road; sun protection, a hat and a water bottle, because the summers can be hot; a small first-aid kit for feet; a head torch and earplugs for shared rooms; and something dry to sleep in. A phone with an offline map is a good tool and a poor single plan, so know your next town before the battery is low. Leave whatever you are unsure of at home.
Money, language and the clock
Portugal and Spain both use the euro. Carry some coins and small notes for small purchases. Prices are not in this book; the people you meet will tell you what things cost.

Portuguese is spoken on the Portuguese side. In Galicia there are two official languages, Galician and Spanish, and you will meet Galician on signs and in place names such as O Porriño and A Escravitude. Pilgrims need little:
bom dia
("good morning" in Portuguese),
obrigado
(a man says thank you) or
obrigada
(a woman does), and in Galicia
grazas
or
gracias
. Say them with a smile and you will be understood.
Remember the clock. Portugal keeps Western European Time, and Galicia Central European Time, one hour ahead. Your phone will change at the border, and your breakfast plan should change with it.
Emergencies
The European emergency number is 112, in Portugal as in Spain. Keep it in your head, not just in your phone.

chapters.title: Porto and northern Portugal: Days 1 to 3

spans.t: The character of these days

The first three days take you out of a big city, through the countryside of northern Portugal, to one of the oldest towns in the country. The first day is the least romantic of the walk. The second has a Romanesque church and a legend about a rooster. The third is the longest day in the book.

A note on the figures. This book found no official stage table for the Portuguese side that it could read, so these distances are lengths measured along the OpenStreetMap route, as recorded in the CaminoPlus catalog notes, and compared with the figures of published guides. They agree to within ~2 km. Treat every one as a good guide, not as a measurement.
Day 1: Porto to Vilarinho (~27 km)

You start at the Sé, the cathedral of Porto. Wikipedia says the present building was begun in the second half of the twelfth century and was worked on until the sixteenth. It has a Romanesque rose window above a Baroque porch, and it has an English footnote: Wikipedia records that King John I of Portugal married Philippa of Lancaster there in 1387. Ask before you leave the city where to get your first stamp.

Then the city lets go of you slowly. The Confraternity of St James says that the Central and Coastal routes alike spend their first day walking through the urban and industrial sprawl of Porto, and that is the honest summary. The way passes Moreira da Maia, which published guides use as the halfway point, then Vilar de Pinheiro and Aldeia Nova, and ends at Vilarinho, a hamlet in the municipality of Vila do Conde. Portugal has many places called Vilarinho; check that yours is the right one.

The distance is ~27 km along the OpenStreetMap route, and published guides give ~26 to ~27 km. It is a long first day on a hard surface, so go slowly and take your breaks early. If it is too much, know that one published plan, which counts twelve stages for the whole route, divides Porto to Barcelos into three days instead of two.

Watch the arrows. The Confraternity says yellow arrows are plentiful from the cathedral to the border, and that blue arrows, which sometimes run beside them, point back towards Porto: they mark the route from Santiago to Porto and on to Fátima. Follow the yellow. Somewhere in this stretch the Coastal Way parts from the Central route; Wikipedia puts the split in the countryside of Vila do Conde. That road is the subject of
The Coastal Way
, and here you stay with the arrows of the Central route.
Day 2: Vilarinho to Barcelos (~27 km)

The way passes Arcos and then São Pedro de Rates, which Wikipedia calls a central place of the Portuguese Way and the place where pilgrims were most numerous. The Romanesque church of Rates has been a national monument since 1910. Wikipedia says its rebuilding began around 1100, when Henry, Count of Portugal, brought in Benedictine monks from France, and counts it among the oldest Romanesque churches in Portugal. According to legend the church honours Peter of Rates, a first bishop of Braga ordained by St James himself; the relics were moved to Braga cathedral in 1552. On the way to Rates, Wikipedia mentions the medieval Dom Zameiro bridge, rebuilt in 1185 on a Roman road.

From Rates the way goes on through Pedra Furada and Carvalhal. Barcelos comes at the end of the day, and the road enters it across the Gothic bridge over the Cávado, built, Wikipedia says, between 1325 and 1328. Barcelos has been a stop for pilgrims since the Middle Ages, and it is the home of a famous legend. Wikipedia tells it in several versions. In one, a Galician pilgrim on his way to Santiago was wrongly accused of a crime and condemned to hang. He asked to see the judge, who was at dinner, and said that the roasted rooster on the table would crow to prove his innocence. As he was hanged, the bird stood up and crowed; the knot had not tightened, and the pilgrim was freed. He later raised a stone cross there in thanks. The rooster of Barcelos is often seen as a symbol of Portugal. The town is also known for its pottery figurines of farmers, musicians and nativity scenes, and Wikipedia says it belongs to UNESCO's Creative Cities Network as a Crafts and Folk Art City.

Around Barcelos, the Confraternity says, you will also see the red and white marks of the long-distance footpath GR11-E9. Follow the yellow arrows. The day is ~27 km along the OpenStreetMap route, against ~26 to ~28 km in published guides.
Day 3: Barcelos to Ponte de Lima (~34 km)

This is the longest day of the book, ~34 km along the OpenStreetMap route and ~34 to ~35 km in published guides. Decide before you start whether to walk it whole. A fit walker with an early start can. Published guides say it can be split in two, around the middle of the day. The way passes Lijó, Aborim and Balugães, and later Vitorino dos Piães, Facha and Correlhã, and goes over a ridge by the pass of Portela de Tamel, which a published guide names. The app and local advice will tell you which villages offer a bed for the night.

If you walk it whole, treat it as a long day and nothing more: breakfast at first light, water at every chance, lunch you have already bought, a hat and a plan for the heat. Heat is the main danger on a day like this: the record high at Porto airport is ~38.6 °C. If you are tired by the middle of the day, the middle of the day is the time to stop.

Ponte de Lima rewards the effort. Wikipedia calls it the oldest chartered town in Portugal and dates its first charter to 4 March 1125. It takes its name from its bridge over the Lima, which Wikipedia says may go back to the first century and was rebuilt in 1125. The Xunta places the Roman road Via XIX through Ponte de Lima, and Wikipedia connects the Roman bridge with it.

There is also an old story about this river. Wikipedia reports that in antiquity the Lima was said to cause loss of memory, and that Strabo compared it to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness; it suggests that Roman soldiers feared crossing it during the conquest of the region in 136 BC. It is a good place to remember why you started, and a safe one to forget your blisters.

chapters.title: The Minho and the border: Days 4 and 5

spans.t: The character of these days

Two shorter days, with the border in the second. The first climbs over the Labruja hills and ends in the village of Rubiães; the second goes down to the Minho, passes a fortress town, crosses a river that is also a frontier, and ends in a Galician town with a cathedral. Between them you leave one country, one language and one clock behind.
The distances are measured along the OpenStreetMap route, as in the previous chapter, and compared with published guides.
Day 4: Ponte de Lima to Rubiães (~18 km)

After the long day to Ponte de Lima, this is a short one, ~18 km along the OpenStreetMap route and in published guides alike. Do not be fooled by the figure. Wikipedia says that one of the most tiring parts of the inland Portuguese Way lies in the Labruja hills, in the municipality of Ponte de Lima, which are hard to cross. The route leaves the river valley by Arcozelo and Labruja and climbs.

Take it as a day of two halves. Start early, with water, and leave the afternoon free. A steady pace uphill is better than a quick start and a long rest. What goes up comes down, to the valley of the little river Coura.

Rubiães is a village, and your last night in Portugal on this plan. It has an old road to show you. Wikipedia describes the bridge of Rubiães as a Roman bridge over the Coura, built in the second century, on the Portuguese Way. The Xunta says that the Roman road Via XIX, which linked Braga with Astorga, ran through Ponte de Lima and Tui, and Rubiães lies between them. It is a good place to rest your feet.
Day 5: Rubiães to Tui (~21 km)

This is the day you cross the border. The distance is ~21 km along the OpenStreetMap route, against ~19 km in one published plan that also ends in Tui. Published guides end the day at Valença, which is ~4 km before Tui, and begin the next from there: they put Rubiães to Valença at ~16 to ~17 km. The CaminoPlus stage list ends the day in Tui.

The way passes Cossourado, Fontoura and Arão, then comes to Valença. Wikipedia says that the town is walled, on the left bank of the Minho, and that its first walls were built in the thirteenth century and its present bastions in the seventeenth and eighteenth. Two polygons of walls stand on two small hills, and inside them, Wikipedia says, a Roman milestone marks the forty-second mile of the road from Braga to Tui. If you have time, walk in through the Porta do Sol, the Gate of the Sun, the main entrance. The view from the ramparts runs across the river to Galicia. Wikipedia says the town was populated by King Sancho I in the twelfth century and was called Contrasta, "village opposed to another", because Tui stood opposite.

Then the border. The Xunta says that the route enters Galicia by the International Bridge, which links Valença and Tui across the powerful Minho. Wikipedia says that the bridge carries a road and a railway and that both countries are in the Schengen area, so there are normally no formalities at the crossing. Stop in the middle: behind you is Portugal, and ahead of you is the Galician stretch of the road.
Remember the clock: Galicia is one hour ahead of Portugal.

Tui sits on a hill above the river. The Xunta calls it one of the seven capitals of the ancient Kingdom of Galicia, and says the town was declared an area of artistic and historical importance in 1967. The cathedral of Santa María, which Wikipedia dates from the eleventh to the thirteenth century, has Romanesque and Gothic parts; the Xunta says it presides over the medieval street plan. Peter González, the Dominican friar known as San Telmo and patron of sailors, died in Tui in 1246 and is buried in the cathedral, Wikipedia says. Near the entrance to the old town the Xunta notes a milestone showing ~115 km to Santiago; north of Tui the Confraternity says you will again see the red and white marks of a long-distance footpath beside the yellow arrows.
Tonight your credencial is about to carry the stamp of a second country.

chapters.title: Galicia, from Tui to Pontevedra: Days 6 to 8

spans.t: The character of these days

The next six days are Galicia, and the Xunta de Galicia describes them in six official stages from Tui to Santiago. This chapter has the first three: through the granite country around O Porriño, along the busy N-550 corridor, and down to the head of the Ría de Vigo, a long sea inlet, before the road turns inland to Pontevedra.

The Galician distances come from the Xunta. Its route page gives ~119 km for the whole Galician Way; its stage pages add up to a little more, ~120 km; and the OpenStreetMap route measured in the CaminoPlus catalog notes differs from the Xunta by no more than ~2.5 km on any stage. Treat each figure as a good guide, not as a measurement.
Day 6: Tui to O Porriño (~18 km)

The Xunta gives this stage as ~18 km and rates it Low, with an estimate of ~3 h 35 min. Its own page disagrees with itself: it marks each of the three sections of the stage Medium-High. Take the first full day in Spain gently.

You leave Tui through its historic quarter to San Bartolomé Park, where a pre-Romanesque church stands. Then comes country. The way passes the chapel of A Virxe do Camiño, the Virgin of the Way, and the bridge the Xunta calls the San Telmo bridge, also known as As Febres, then runs through a dense wood called A Ribeira to the small village of A Madanela. The Louro, the little river that divides the municipalities of Tui and O Porriño, runs beside the path. At Orbenlle the Xunta says you can continue by Os Eidos or by As Gándaras.

In the distance you can see the granite quarries that have made this place famous. The Xunta says the stone is known as pink granite and is exported to places as far away as the United States and Japan.

O Porriño is an industrial town, as the Xunta says, with one of the highest rates of population growth in the province of Pontevedra. Its look is the work of the architect Antonio Palacios, who was born there in 1874; the Town Hall, one of his greatest works, dates from 1924. The Xunta also points to the Templete de la Red de San Luis, which was once the entrance to a Madrid underground station, and to the fountain of O Cristo, dated 1907. It is a working town more than a postcard. Rest your feet and prepare for tomorrow.
Day 7: O Porriño to Redondela (~16 km)

The Xunta gives ~16 km and rates the stage Low, with an estimate of ~3 h 10 min. Its three sections add up to ~15 km, so the page differs from itself by about a kilometre. The OpenStreetMap route comes to ~16 km as well.

This day has the road in it, and the Xunta is plain about it. After the chapel of As Angustias the way runs along the N-550, and the Xunta says it is especially important to watch for vehicles; a way that diverts to the right avoids the traffic. The Louro can be heard but not seen. You pass A Rúa, once the municipal capital of Mos, where a stone cross inscribed "Camino de Santiago" marks the street that leads to a cross monument. At O Enxertado there is a slight climb to the small chapel of Santiaguiño de Anta, in an oak wood, the
carballeira

Then the old road shows itself. The Xunta says that a Roman milestone, one Roman mile being about 1,480 metres, guides you towards Redondela. It once belonged to Via XIX, the road linking Braga and Astorga. The woods are pine and eucalyptus, and the section ends at a place the Xunta calls legendary, Chan das Pipas. Saxamonde, Quintela and O Muro lead to Redondela, which you enter by the Ponteareas Square.

Redondela is known as the village of the viaducts, Wikipedia says, for its two railway viaducts of the nineteenth century. It is also where another road joins yours. The Xunta says that the coastal variant of the Portuguese Way, which crosses the Minho at A Guarda, meets the inland route here. From Redondela on, those who came by the sea and those who came by the Central route share one path. That coastal road is the subject of
The Coastal Way
Day 8: Redondela to Pontevedra (~18 km)

The Xunta gives ~18 km, rates the stage Medium and estimates ~4 h 35 min. The OpenStreetMap route is longer, ~20 km, and published guides give ~18 to ~19 km. This is the largest gap on the Galician side, so allow for a longer day than the Xunta's.

The first half belongs to the water. After the chapel of As Angustias, in the parish of Cesantes, the Ría de Vigo opens on your left. The Xunta points to the islands of San Simón and San Antón, and says that the remains of the galleons of the Battle of Rande, fought in 1702, lie beneath the water. Rande Bridge, a cable-stayed bridge, rises above the rafts of the mussel farmers. Then comes Arcade, and the way follows its streets down to the medieval Sampaio Bridge over the Verdugo. The municipality of Pontevedra begins at the middle of the bridge.

After Ponte Sampaio the road climbs along ancient stone paths. The Xunta says that these include sections of the Roman Via XIX, such as the climb of the Brea Vella de A Canicouva. Then the way approaches Pontevedra by several small places, among them Santa Comba de Bértola and Tomeza, and enters the city, passing the shrine of the Pilgrim Virgin on the way to the old quarter.

Pontevedra is a place to stay a second night. Wikipedia says its old town is the second most important historic centre in Galicia, after Santiago, and that the city has pedestrianised its centre. The circular church of the Pilgrim Virgin, which Wikipedia dates to the eighteenth century, has a floor plan in the shape of a scallop shell. Wikipedia adds that the carrack Santa María, one of Columbus's ships, originally named La Gallega, was built in Pontevedra. You will cross the medieval Burgo Bridge tomorrow; Wikipedia says there are scallop shells carved in its arches.

chapters.title: Galicia, from Pontevedra to Santiago: Days 9 to 11

spans.t: The character of these days

The last three days are the longest run of Galician walking: ~23 km, ~19 km and ~25 km. The road leaves Pontevedra over a medieval bridge, follows a thread of villages, stone crosses and small rivers to a spa town on the Umia, crosses the Ulla into the province of A Coruña, and climbs the last hills to the cathedral. The figures are the Xunta's, with the OpenStreetMap route as a cross-check, and they agree closely.
Day 9: Pontevedra to Caldas de Reis (~23 km)
The Xunta gives ~23 km, rates the stage Medium and estimates ~5 h 45 min. The OpenStreetMap route is ~21 km and published guides say ~23 km, so plan for the longer figure.

You leave Pontevedra by the street called A Santiña, after crossing the Lérez on the Burgo Bridge. The way runs beside a large wetland, A Xunqueira de Alba, between the railway and the river Granda, and climbs to the church of Santa María de Alba. The Xunta says that Diego Gelmírez, the archbishop of Santiago, once stopped at Guxilde on his way from Braga to Compostela. The Pilgrim's Office credits him with the energetic promotion of the pilgrimage in the early twelfth century.

Then come woods, the leafy ones of Reirís and Lombo da Maceira, a small stone bridge into the municipality of Barro, and the village of Valbón among large stone houses. The Xunta singles out three stone crosses beside the way: one near a house, one with a carving of St James the Pilgrim on its shaft, looking north towards Compostela, and the solitary cross of Soutelo. It calls them a triad of sculptures made to mark crossroads.

After Valbón, the Xunta says, you need to watch the signs closely. The route meanders, meets other paths, and has the N-550 as a constant companion, and a new high-speed rail line has altered the landscape. Take care at junctions.

Caldas de Reis is a spa town. The Xunta says it is the Aquae Celenis of the Antonine Itinerary, a third-century record of Roman roads, and Wikipedia adds that the older name means "hot springs". The Umia and the Bermaña run through it. The road crosses a bridge over the Umia, which leads to the hot spring that has given the town its name since Roman times, and then a medieval bridge over the Bermaña. The chapel of San Roque marks the end of the stage.
Day 10: Caldas de Reis to Padrón (~19 km)
The Xunta gives ~19 km, rates the stage Medium and estimates ~4 h 45 min. The OpenStreetMap route and published guides all fall within a kilometre of that, so on this day the figures agree.

The path runs through Casalderrique and Casal de Eirigo and enters the municipality of Valga. Mount Castelo follows, dense woods watered by the Valga river and dotted with old mills. The Xunta then lists Cimadevilla, the bridge over the Fontenlo and the villages of Cedelo and Condide, in Pontecesures. The Pino Manso viewpoint looks over the valley of the Ulla.

You cross the Ulla by a bridge that was originally Roman and is now much changed. The Xunta says this river is the boundary between the provinces of Pontevedra and A Coruña, so the end of the day is a provincial boundary as well as a river. On the far side is Padrón, which the Xunta calls the home of the Jacobean tradition. Its church of Santiago keeps the Pedrón, a Roman altar stone with a carved cross that, the Xunta says, is said to have been added by the disciples of St James.
The tradition has a story attached. Wikipedia says that, according to tradition, the disciples Theodore and Athanasius brought the body of St James from Jerusalem in a stone boat and moored it to a
pedrón

, a big stone, which gave the place its name. The Xunta tells the same story in its description of the sea and river route that follows the apostle's last journey: the body came by sea to the Ría de Arousa and up the Ulla to Padrón, the river harbour of the Roman city of Iria Flavia. It is a tradition, not a record. Whether or not you hold it, it explains why this small town matters.

Padrón is also known for its small green peppers, and Wikipedia quotes the Galician saying that some are hot and some are not. It says Padrón has been home to four important writers, among them the Romantic poet Rosalía de Castro, who lived from 1837 to 1885, and the Nobel laureate Camilo José Cela, who lived from 1916 to 2002.
Day 11: Padrón to Santiago de Compostela (~25 km)

The last day is ~25 km by the Xunta, which rates it Low and estimates ~5 h. The OpenStreetMap route agrees at ~25 km. It is the longest day of the Galician stages, and it ends with a cathedral. Start early so that you arrive with time to spare and not with the light going.

You leave by Dolores Street and cross the Sar to Iria Flavia. The Xunta says it was once a Roman city and an episcopal see until the eleventh century. Beyond it is the foundation of the Nobel laureate Camilo José Cela, who is buried opposite. The way crosses the N-550, and again the Xunta says you can take the branch to the right to avoid the traffic.

The Sar valley follows, with its small villages, and then the sanctuary of A Escravitude, with views over the valleys of Padrón. The path goes on past O Faramello and over the hills to O Milladoiro. The Xunta says that the name is the
humilladoiro

, the place where pilgrims knelt, humbled, on first catching sight of the cathedral; and that here Compostela can already be breathed. Whether you see the towers from there depends on the weather and the day. Slow down anyway.

Then you drop to A Rocha Vella and cross the Sar by the Old Bridge. The route follows the river, and at a fork there are two clearly signed ways, which meet again at Rosalía de Castro Street. The old quarter is entered by the Porta Faxeira and O Franco Street. The Xunta says the traditional entrance to the cathedral for pilgrims on the Portuguese Way is through As Praterías Square, and Wikipedia says the cathedral's Praterías façade was built by Master Esteban in 1103.
Take the last hundred metres slowly.

chapters.title: Other ways to split the days, other roads, and the Compostela rule

spans.t: Other ways to split the days

The eleven days in this book are the CaminoPlus stage list. They are not the only plan: the CaminoPlus route list gives twelve stages and its stage list eleven, because published plans do not agree. Here are the commonest changes.

items.t: Start in Galicia.
The Xunta de Galicia describes six stages from Tui to Santiago, which are Days 6 to 11 of this book. They total ~119 km by the Xunta's figures, and they make a walk of six days.
End Day 5 in Valença.
Published guides stop at Valença, ~4 km before Tui, and start the next day there. They put Rubiães to Valença at ~16 to ~17 km, and Valença to O Porriño at ~20 km.
Three days to Barcelos.
One published plan divides Porto to Barcelos into three shorter days instead of two. If the first day's ~27 km worries you, this is the plan to look for.
Split the long Day 3.

Published guides divide Barcelos to Ponte de Lima around the middle of the day, near Vitorino dos Piães, and the app and local advice will tell you what is open for the night. A split makes it roughly two days of ~17 km.
Add a rest day.
Pontevedra is the natural place, as its entry says. Ponte de Lima and Padrón are others.

spans.t: Whatever you choose, the arithmetic is the same: eleven days, ~246 km on this book's figures, so ~22 km a day on average, less on the days that are short.
Other roads: the Coastal Way and the Spiritual Variant
This book describes only the Central route. The
Coastal Way

is another road to the same city. The Xunta says that its variant crosses the Minho at A Guarda and rejoins the inland route at Redondela, and the Confraternity says it leaves the Central route near Porto and follows the shore. It has its own book in this series,
The Coastal Way
, for those who want the sea.
The
Spiritual Variant

is a sea-and-river alternative that leaves the Central route at Pontevedra. The Confraternity describes it as a relatively new variant that goes to Vilanova de Arousa, on the shores of the Sea of Arousa, then takes a boat up the estuary to Pontecesures and rejoins the Central route to Santiago. The Xunta describes a related maritime and river itinerary, the Mar de Arousa and Río Ulla Route, which commemorates the arrival of the body of St James by sea, and says that the walk from Padrón to Santiago is ~25 km. A route that depends on a boat depends on the boat: ask locally before you plan around it.
The Confraternity says that most pilgrims start in Porto but many walk from Lisbon. The catalog lists that route at ~620 km, and it reaches Porto first. It is not in this book.
The Compostela rule

The Compostela is the certificate the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback. The Office asks for at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred kilometres by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route. On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that it recognises. The final stage must include at least the last one leading into the Cathedral.

The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

The Way may be done in stages, if they follow in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and the end of each stage, with the date. A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain. The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.

Here is the arithmetic for this road, with its sources. The Xunta gives the Galician Way from Tui as ~119 km, and a milestone it notes in Tui reads ~115 km to Santiago. Wikipedia gives figures from ~107 to ~116 km in different articles. All of them are more than a hundred kilometres, but by a margin that depends on the source and on where you start counting. If you walk from Porto, the Spanish stretch alone is ~119 km on the Xunta's figures, which is more than the seventy kilometres in Spain that the Office names for those who have walked a recognised route outside Spain.
None of that is a decision. The Office decides, and rules change. If you plan to start in Tui, in Valença or anywhere near the limit, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and often a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office lists access to "hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first practical use of the credencial, and notes that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

Which hostels exist, which are open this month, whether you may book a bed and how beds are given out differ from town to town and change from season to season. This book does not list them. Use the CaminoPlus app for where to sleep tonight, ask locally for tomorrow, and do not rely on one source for a long day, such as Day 3.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and do not rustle bags at night or before dawn. Pack your rucksack in the hall.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed. Shoes belong where the house puts them.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.
Keep your valuables close.

spans.t: Bedbugs

are a risk in any shared bed anywhere. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack and clothes off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Some places along the Way offer a
menú del peregrino
, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it and what it costs before you sit. A set meal is a good way to eat well after a long day, and an easy way to try what the region cooks.
You will pass through two food cultures, and it is worth tasting both. Wikipedia lists the dishes of Valença, the last town in Portugal:
lampreia à minhota
, lamprey; goat; salt cod; and the
empanada
, a pie of meat or fish. In Galicia it is hard to miss the green peppers of Padrón, fried in olive oil and coarse salt. Wikipedia says that the heat of the pepper varies from one to the next.
You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.
Water matters as much. Fill your bottle in each town, and carry something for lunch on the long days: Day 3 in Portugal and Days 9 and 11 in Galicia.
Resting
It is easy to treat the walk as a timetable to be kept. Resist that. A day of rest is part of the walk.

If you have a day to spare, Pontevedra is a good place to spend it: Wikipedia says that its old town is the second most important historic centre in Galicia and that the centre is pedestrianised. Ponte de Lima, at the end of the longest day, is another candidate. The other place is the end. Santiago is a city built for the end of a pilgrimage, and it deserves more than a night.

On the road, listen to your body before you listen to your plan. Take the short days as short days. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
Feet

Look after your feet first. Take your shoes off at lunch and let your feet breathe. Change your socks. Treat a hot spot at once, before it is a blister. On a road with this much hard surface, cushioning matters, so spend money on good shoes and time on breaking them in.
Heat

The summers can be hot. The record highs are ~38.6 °C at Porto airport and ~39.4 °C at Santiago airport, and the Confraternity of St James warns of heat with high humidity. Start early, carry more water than you think you need, wear a hat, and plan the hot hours for shade and rest. Day 3, ~34 km, is the day to think about it most. If you feel dizzy, sick or confused, stop in the shade, drink, and ask for help; if it does not pass, call 112.
Rain

This is a wet road. Santiago gets ~1,500 to ~1,800 mm of rain a year, depending on the source, and the Confraternity says that in periods of low pressure the rain can be heavy and prolonged. A rain jacket and a cover for your pack are not optional, and a spare pair of dry socks in a plastic bag is the cheapest comfort on the road. Rain on a long day is also a reason to take a shorter one.
Roads and paths

The Portuguese Way meets main roads. The Confraternity says it often joins them at the entrance and exit of towns and advises that, when using roads, you watch for traffic and use the indicated strip between the road and the drainage ditch. In Galicia the Xunta warns of the N-550 on Day 7 and Day 11 and says there are branches to the right that take you off the traffic. It describes the N-550 on Day 9 as a constant presence, with a new high-speed rail line that has altered the landscape, and asks you to watch the signs closely.
Where there is no path, walk facing the traffic, in single file, and never in the dark. Do not take a shortcut on a main road to save a kilometre.

Look at the arrows at every junction. Blue arrows, which the Confraternity says point back towards Porto, are not yours; yellow ones are. Around Barcelos and north of Tui you will also see the red and white marks of a long-distance footpath; they are a different route.
Border and papers

Wikipedia says that Portugal and Spain are both signatories of the Schengen Treaty, so there are normally no formalities at the Minho. Carry your passport or identity card anyway, as you should in any country, and remember the clock changes.
When to stop

Stop when something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, when you are dizzy, when the weather turns, or when the light is going. A short day costs you an afternoon; a bad decision can cost you the Camino. Tell someone your plan. The emergency number is 112, in Portugal and in Spain.
Before you go, check for diversions, closures and, in summer, heat and fire warnings. A route can change between this book's date and your walk.
Why people walk

People walk this road for faith, for sport, for grief, for curiosity, for a rest from work, for a promise made to someone else. The Pilgrim's Office asks that the Compostela be sought for religious and/or spiritual reasons, and says so plainly; the road itself asks nothing of the kind. Every reason is a good one, and none of them needs to be explained to the people you meet.

The people before you had every kind of reason too. The Xunta names queens and kings, Elizabeth of Portugal and Manuel I among them. It adds that in the nineteenth century, the century of the fewest pilgrims, more than eighty per cent of the foreign pilgrims were Portuguese. This was a road ordinary people took, as well as royalty.
What the road gives
It gives you hours with no task. For eleven days the feet, the weather and the next town set the agenda, and what you do with the quiet is yours.
It also has places that seem made for thinking. A river that, Wikipedia reports, the ancients said took away memory. A border in the middle of a bridge. A hill, the
humilladoiro
, where the Xunta says pilgrims once knelt on first catching sight of their goal. You need not believe a legend to be moved by the hour in which you stand where people have stood for centuries.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, or none. They are better walked than answered.

items.t: What are you carrying that is not in your pack?
Whom would you like to have beside you on this road, and what would you say to them?
What do you want to remember from today, and what would you like to forget, as the old story says the Lima could make a pilgrim forget?
What would "enough" look like today, for your feet and for your heart?
What are you walking towards, and what are you walking away from? Is the second a reason to turn round, or only a reason to keep going?

spans.t: You do not have to arrive at an answer in Santiago. A better question is a fair thing to bring home.
The cathedral

The Portuguese Way ends where every Way ends: at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, the reputed burial place of St James. Wikipedia dates the start of construction to 1075. It is a Romanesque building with later Gothic and Baroque additions. The Xunta says the traditional entrance for pilgrims on the Portuguese Way is through As Praterías Square, and Wikipedia says that the cathedral's Praterías façade was built in 1103. The great Baroque façade on the Praza do Obradoiro, the square in front, was completed in 1740. Inside, the Pórtico da Gloria, the carved Romanesque doorway by Master Mateo, carries the date 1188, according to Wikipedia. The old town was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985.

The cathedral keeps a Holy Door, opened only in a Jacobean Holy Year, and the next Holy Year is 2027, then 2032. It also keeps the botafumeiro, the great censer, which Wikipedia says is swung on certain important religious holidays, and at every Pilgrims' Mass in a Holy Year.
Take a moment in the square before you do anything else. Sit on the stones if you like. The arrival may be quieter or noisier than you expected; there is no right feeling.
The Pilgrim's Office and the Compostela
The
Compostela

is the certificate of your pilgrimage, written in Latin, and the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues it. The rule it follows is in the chapter on other ways to split the days, and it is the Office's to apply. The Latin text speaks of those who come
devotionis affectu, voti vel pietatis
, which the Office's own English version renders as coming "with an attitude of devotion or because of a vow or promise".

Bring your credencial, stamped along the way. You also take a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue on your phone. The Office warns that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee that you will receive the Compostela on the same day, so do not book a flight home for the afternoon. The Office's website gives its address and its current hours, which are not in this book because they change.
If you walked for other reasons, or are not sure that yours count, the Office also offers a separate
certificate of distance

. It records where you began, how many kilometres you travelled, the dates and the route, whatever your starting point. It carries a fee, and the Office gives the amount. The Office says its reception service and the Compostela itself are free.
The Office meets a great many people in a day. Be patient, be warm, and if you have a doubt about your credencial, ask before you queue.
The pilgrims' Mass

The cathedral holds a Pilgrims' Mass. Check the cathedral's own website for the time, which changes. You do not need to be a believer to sit at the back and listen. It is a cathedral full of people who have walked.
The next day

Try not to leave on the morning after you arrive. A day in Santiago lets the walk settle. Wash your clothes, sleep late, and look at the old town. On the cathedral square stands a building that the Catholic Monarchs founded as a royal hospital for pilgrims; the Office says that those who showed their Compostela there once had the right to stay three days free, and that it has been a hotel since 1954.

If you still have legs and time, some pilgrims walk on to Finisterre and Muxía on the coast, ~90 km farther, a route you will find in the CaminoPlus app's list. If you do not, think about the way home: Santiago has an airport ~12 km from the city, and the Confraternity of St James notes a bus service of about four hours to Porto. Check the current times. And buy a postcard, and write to someone you walked with in your head.

The first days back are strange. The road has taught your body a rhythm of early light, one thing at a time and a short list of needs, and home does not run on it. Expect to miss the walking before you miss anything else.

Keep what you can. Walk to the shop and not to the car. Eat one meal a day without a screen, as the road suggested. Write down three things you want to remember before they blur: a bridge, a face, a hill. Put the credencial somewhere you will see it. A stamp is a small thing, and a full card of them is a map of a fortnight you will not live again in quite that way.
Tell the story, and listen when someone else tells theirs. Every pilgrim has one, and every one is different.

If you want to walk again, the road has neighbours. The Coastal Way, in this series, goes from Porto to Santiago beside the sea. The walk from Santiago to Finisterre and Muxía, ~90 km in the catalog, goes on to the ocean. The French Way, ~773 km, is a longer commitment. The CaminoPlus app lists them all.
Whatever you do next, thank the people who kept the road open for you: the friends of the Camino, the hosts and the people in the villages.
Bom caminho
, and
Buen Camino
, again.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus
. The app is still in development, so look in the app for what is available on the Camino Portugués today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.
A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in any app is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.
Sources and thanks
This book rests on public sources, and the fact ledger that goes with it lists every fact against the page it came from. The chief ones are:

items.t: The Xunta de Galicia

, the regional government, on its official Camino de Santiago portal (caminodesantiago.gal): the page on the Portuguese Way, its six stages from Tui to Santiago with their lengths and descriptions, and the page on the Mar de Arousa and Río Ulla Route.
The Pilgrim's Reception Office of the Cathedral of Santiago
(oficinadelperegrino.com): the rules of the Compostela, the credencial, the certificate of distance and the history of the pilgrimage.
The Confraternity of St James
(csj.org.uk): its page on the Camino Portugués, for the route, the waymarking, the weather and the way out of Porto.
Wikipedia

, for history, geography and climate: the articles on the Portuguese Way, Porto, its cathedral and its airport, Barcelos, Ponte de Lima, Valença, the monastery church of Rates, the bridge of Rubiães, Tui, Peter González, Redondela, Pontevedra, Caldas de Reis, Padrón, Santiago de Compostela, its cathedral and its airport, the Jacobean Holy Year, Galicia, Portugal and time in Portugal and Spain. It is also where this book found the Pilgrim's Office statistics for 2025, and the climate averages of the Portuguese and Spanish weather services.
Published day-length tables
for Porto, checked against a standard solar calculation, for the hours of daylight.
The CaminoPlus route catalog
, for the names and order of the eleven stages and, for the Portuguese days, lengths measured along the OpenStreetMap route (data by OpenStreetMap contributors) and compared with published guides.
The Associação dos Amigos do Caminho Português de Santiago
, which the Confraternity credits for the yellow arrows between Porto and the border.

spans.t: Stage lengths differ from one source to the next, and a few pages disagree with themselves, so every distance in this book is marked ~. This book found no official stage table for Portugal that it could read; the Portuguese figures are therefore the least certain. If you know a better figure, or a fact that has changed, tell CaminoPlus.
Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the towns and villages who point the way and say
bom caminho
to a stranger.
A short glossary

items.t: Albergue
: a pilgrims' hostel with shared rooms.
Botafumeiro
: the great censer of Santiago cathedral.
Bom caminho, Buen Camino
: "good Way", the greeting between pilgrims, in Portuguese and in Spanish.
Caminho, Camino
: "way" or "road", in Portuguese and in Spanish.
Carballeira
: an oak wood, in Galician.
Carimbo, sello
: a stamp in the credencial, in Portuguese and in Spanish.
Compostela
: the Latin certificate the Pilgrim's Office issues.
Credencial
: the pilgrim's passport.
Hospitalero
: the host of a pilgrims' hostel.
Humilladoiro
: the place where pilgrims knelt on first seeing the cathedral, in Galician.
Menú del peregrino
: a set meal for pilgrims.
Peregrino
: a pilgrim.
Pedrón
: the big stone of Padrón.
Ría
: a long sea inlet, as at Vigo and Pontevedra.
Sé
: the cathedral, in Portuguese.
Xunta
: the regional government of Galicia.
